summary:
Rivers State has no statute, policy or enforcement practice of its own on same-sex conduct or gender expression in the sources reviewed. The state stands under Nigeria's national framework, which applies nationwide; its provisions and penalties are set out in the national assessment. The layer that varies by geography is the criminal code in force across southern Nigeria, and it applies in Rivers: sex between men carries up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency up to 3 years. Rivers is not among the northern states where Sharia provisions apply, so the death-penalty exposure those states attach to same-sex conduct does not arise for a visitor to Port Harcourt or elsewhere in the state.

The sources place one documented incident inside Rivers. In January 2015 a 21-year-old man from Lagos travelled to Port Harcourt to meet a person he had contacted on Facebook and was attacked and sexually abused there. He did not report the attack to the police. The sources record no arrest, charge or official response in connection with it.

Beyond that case, the sources identify no Rivers prosecution, arrest, police operation or state-government statement on same-sex conduct or gender expression, and no enforcement pattern specific to the state. No Rivers institution appears in the sources as either hostile or protective, and no trans-specific incident, facility rule or care restriction particular to Rivers is recorded.
tangentialFactors:
Rivers sits in the southern belt where the criminal code applies, in contrast to the northern states where Sharia provisions carry penalties up to death for same-sex conduct. A visitor moving between the two parts of Nigeria crosses a change in the maximum penalty, not merely in enforcement intensity.

The single Rivers incident in the sources is a 2015 attack on a visitor from another state, so the state's documented record rests on one case rather than a series. The national framework applies uniformly to Rivers, which means the statutory exposure a visitor faces in Port Harcourt is the same as in any other southern state; what differs is the local record of enforcement, which the sources leave thin.
localsOnly:
Rivers State has enacted no law, policy or programme of its own on same-sex conduct or gender expression in the sources reviewed, in either direction: no state-level criminal provision beyond the national framework and no state-level protection. Residents rely on the same national statute as visitors.

The sources record no Rivers court decision, no Rivers prosecution and no state-government statement on the subject. The 2015 Port Harcourt attack was not reported to the police, and the sources record no investigation into it.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Rivers police or courts have applied the national statute or the southern criminal code in any specific case is not documented in the sources. No Rivers case law, charge sheet or conviction is available.

Whether Rivers courts apply the 2022 nationwide ruling that struck down three provisions of the SSMPA is not documented. The sources do not establish how state-level prosecutors or police treat that ruling.

The sources hold no data on trans residents or visitors in Rivers: no count, no recorded trans-specific violence, no facility or documentation practice, and no state-level health or support provision. The sources record no such incidents here, and nothing in them establishes that none have occurred.
